newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Analysts divided on KBB's M&S Mode.
newsitem.headline: Analysts divided on KBB's M&S Mode.

text.p: Analysts on Monday were divided on the prospects of M&S Mode, the loss-making clothing chain of Dutch retail group Koninklijke Bijenkorf Beheer NV (KBB).
KBB issued a profit warning last Friday, blaming a projected sharp decline in 1996/97 results on the losses at M&S Mode.
KBB's 1996/97 ordinary net was set to fall to between 55 and 60 million guilders, from 98.6 million in 1995/96, the company said.
Some analysts feel KBB may now have the worst behind it.
"The bottom may have been reached," said ING Barings' Dennis Jullens, adding he had the impression the company had recognised its problems reasonably quickly.
Bas Nienhaus, analyst at Stroeve, was far more pessimistic.

"There are no incidental costs in these forecasts, they're operational figures. M&S Mode has a structural image problem and I don't expect things to pick up just because the company changes its purchasing team," he said.
He said the new team should get things under control sooner or later, but added he did not expect to see positive effects before 1998.

KBB issued a previous profit warning last October, again blaming the group's problems on the negative trend at M&S Mode, and the chain then decided to increase the flexibility of its product range by modifying its purchasing strategy.
"There's an image problem. To me, it seems doubtful the collection was the only problem area...M&S has to reposition itself," said Joost van Beek from HSBC Van Meer James Capel.
He added that, although the clothing segment itself showed little growth, attractive margins could be generated if the formula was right.
Ab Barneveld from Generale Bank said he expected M&S would still suffer from its unadapted purchasing strategy in the first half of 1997.

"M&S used to be KBB's cash-cow. It won't return to its former profit level before 1998, probably not even before 1999," he said, adding KBB's bottom-line figure was likely to continue suffering from the clothing chain's misfortunes for a while.
The analysts agreed that the trouble at M&S Mode did not mean KBB would shift out of the clothing business.
"KBB indicated years ago it intended to be active with both department stores (mainly in the Netherlands) and speciality stores (also abroad). They will not change this strategy," said Jullens.
"They shelved the expansion plans for M&S Mode until things are back on track again, but have little choice other than to continue the formula," said Van Beek.

However, Barneveld said in the very long term the weight of KBB's clothing business could diminish a little in favour of the do-it-yourself and other speciality stores as expansion possibilities were better in these segments.
